content:
A full Launch Team chart can still leave you doing the work yourself. Names in boxes are not leaders. You spot future leaders by noticing what people already contribute, then handing them a small piece of real work and telling them what you saw.

This is the first move, and it should be broad. Offer small responsibilities across the Core Group. Give feedback. Let any later invitation grow out of that shared work. Do not open by choosing a short list and writing development plans for them. A planned apprenticeship belongs later, after someone has already carried a small responsibility. It is not the way you decide who gets a first chance.

---

## Notice the whole group

Emerging leadership is meant to rise from the Core Group. The Senior Pastor equips those people. At this stage you notice, you ask, and you stay close enough to tell the truth.

Watch contribution, not volume. Who sets up without being asked. Who stays after a Vision Meeting to help a guest find a next step. Who keeps a dull promise. Who asks a careful question instead of taking over the room. Those are reasons to talk. Easy talk in the meeting does not put someone ahead of a person who rarely speaks.

Quieter people still get missed when you only reward voices you already know. That is the real weakness of a broad approach, so plan for it. Once a month, look for someone you have not asked. Look through Worship, Walk, Work, and Witness, including the people who do not sit near you.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"He who is faithful in a very little thing is faithful also in much, and he who is unrighteous in a very little thing is unrighteous also in much."* — Luke 16:10 (LSB)
</Callout>

Peter spreads that work across the group. "As each one has received a gift, employ it in serving one another as good stewards of the manifold grace of God—" 1 Peter 4:10 (LSB). A first chance to serve belongs to the people already in the work with you.

---

## Hand them a small responsibility

Keep the task small enough to finish, and make it real work. Tie it to something they have already shown interest in. A miss should not put Launch Sunday at risk. Tell them the end date when you ask.

These are examples of offers, not a scale.

| What you noticed | Small responsibility | What to discuss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| They welcome guests | Host the welcome table for two Sundays, then debrief | Whether they kept the commitment, and how they treated new people |
| They are steady with children | Assist one children's teacher for a month | Whether they came prepared, and whether they could take a correction |
| They handle details | Own the setup list for one Vision Meeting | Whether the list got done, and whether they asked for help when stuck |

Do not score the row. There is no point value for warmth, skill, or promise. You are collecting something specific to talk about.

A skill, a job history, or a stretch of steady attendance and serving can be a reason to start that talk. None of them establish calling, character, or readiness for a role. Weigh character the way you already do in [the 5 interview criteria](/wiki/frameworks/the-5-interview-criteria). Skill cannot stand in for it.

<Callout type="warning">
A list, a tag, or a leadership candidate signal is not a judgment. Everyfield does not score calling, character, fitness, or spiritual health, and it does not certify anyone for a role. If the product suggests a conversation, a person still has to have that conversation. The suggestion never appoints anyone.
</Callout>

---

## Stay for the feedback

A task with no debrief is how development drifts. Name one person who will follow up with everyone you ask this month. That is often the Senior Pastor. It can be a Launch Team leader who already walks with that part of the group. Name that person. Do not leave follow-up to the group in general, and do not leave it to the product.

Within a week, sit down and say what you saw. "You were on time both Sundays, and you learned the guest's name before you handed them a seat" gives them something to use. "You have a heart for people" does not. Ask what felt heavy. Ask what they would change. Ask whether they want another small task or a pause.

Take the answer. Some faithful people should not move toward a launch role right now. Family load, a hard season, or a young faith are reasons to keep the work small. Say that plainly, so a pause does not sound like a closed door.

<Callout type="tip">
Before the next round of small tasks, write down who has not been asked. If the names are only people you already like being around, you have a short list. You are calling it broad.
</Callout>

---

## Let the next ask grow from the work

A later invitation is a human decision after real work, not a label you applied on the way in. It might be a larger slice of the same area. It might be a conversation about a key role, looking for character, faithfulness, alignment, and coachability, as [Key Leadership Roles Overview](/wiki/launch-team/leadership/key-leadership-roles-overview) already describes. It might be no, or not yet.

Keep that invitation separate from the first task. Two Sundays at the welcome table are not an assimilation appointment. A month assisting in the children's room is not the children's ministry leader role. Say the limit when you ask.

Apprenticeship comes after this, not before it. Small group ministry still names an apprentice when a group is ready to multiply, and the Senior Pastor still equips leaders who have taken a defined area. Start those mentored relationships once shared work has already taught you something. Do not write them for a handful of familiar people and treat everyone else as finished. Early selection favors the people you already know, and the rest of the Core Group hears that leadership is closed.

[The Senior Pastor role](/wiki/launch-team/leadership/senior-pastor-role) includes developing leaders. [The Small Group Leader role](/wiki/launch-team/leadership/small-group-leader-role) includes that later apprentice step. This article stops at the broad offer.

---

## An empty role is a coverage gap

A blank box on the Launch Team chart does not mean the Core Group has no leaders. It means that responsibility has no owner yet. Several people may be able to grow into it. None of them have been asked. Treat the empty role as a coverage gap, then look again.

The other error is a desperation appointment. Do not hand someone a key role because Launch Sunday is close and the box is blank. A wrong leader costs more than a temporary gap. Ask for help on a bounded piece of the empty area, watch it, and talk. If no one is ready, cover the gap yourself or with a short-term helper. Do not invent readiness to make the chart look finished.

---

## Mistakes that shrink the pool

- Watching only the loudest volunteer, and never asking the person who has been faithful off to the side.
- Offering several small tasks and debriefing none of them.
- Using a skill list or a product signal as a score.
- Announcing a larger role before you have talked in private. The Core Group will hear the announcement as the decision.
- Using the small group apprentice plan as the filter for who may try a small task.

<Callout type="insight">
If a role is empty, ask who has carried a small piece of that work and has not been invited to talk. The gap is coverage. It is not proof that leaders are missing.
</Callout>

---

## A conversation you can have this month

- [ ] Pick someone from across the group, including a quiet person.
- [ ] Name the task, the end date, and who will debrief it.
- [ ] Say what this is not. It is not an appointment, and it is not a score.
- [ ] Debrief while the work is fresh. Name one specific thing you saw.
- [ ] Decide together on another small task, a pause, or a separate conversation about a larger role.
- [ ] Write down who owns follow-up, so the offer does not vanish after Sunday.

Then stop. You do not need a private ranking. You need a few honest assignments and a person who will come back and talk.

rulings: Bryan ruled R5 = Option A: "Broad opportunities to develop" (2026-10-26 1:31 PM ET).

Wording call: kept the backlog title Spotting Future Leaders and the slug launch-team/leadership/spotting-future-leaders. In the article, spotting means noticing contributions across the group and offering small responsibilities, not selecting a short list.
Wording call: sort_order 12, one past the highest published article in launch-team/leadership, which is 11. Published rows were not renumbered.

Wording call: omitted the 60-day figure from the body because it has no public URL. The body treats a leadership candidate signal, and steady attendance plus serving, only as a prompt for a human conversation, consistent with Bryan C07 and REQ-TEAM-017. Recorded skills do not establish calling or readiness, consistent with REQ-PPL-011. Interview judgments stay with people, consistent with REQ-PI-007.

Wording call: named apprenticeship only as a later step so the article does not contradict the Playbook small-group apprentice program or the Senior Pastor's charge to equip leaders. The article does not teach a planned apprenticeship as the way to spot leaders.
Wording call: did not name Bryan, requirement IDs, or assessment colors in the reader-facing text. Empty roles are described as a coverage gap, consistent with Bryan C14.
